Good evening. My name is Amy B. Woodman, W-O-O-D-M-A-N. I'm a parent of a third grader, a former teacher at a title I school. I hold the Master's in Education Policy from the University of Michigan, and I'm the president of the Glencoe Elementary PTA. The Glencoe PTA aligns with other PPS communities in desiring a methodical, transparent approach to district right-sizing. I'm asking the board to address an important gap in the current framework that will be shared tonight. It measures how many focal students a scenario affects, but it does not explicitly measure whether those students are succeeding academically or whether a proposed receiving school can sustain their progress. Glenco's results deserve careful examination. I provided a copy to the board manager earlier today. Not only are we a tight-knit neighborhood school with a high teacher retention, our students averaged 81% proficiency in ELA and 76% in math on the ODE report card last year. Glencoe does not qualify as a Title I school, but focal students attend and thrive here. About one in four students is a student of color, one in five has an IEP,

and nearly one in five receives free or reduced lunch. At Glencoe, students with disabilities are 63 percent proficient in ELA and 68 in math compared to the PPS rates of 33 and 29 percent. Students experienced poverty have 50 percent proficiency in ELA and 46 in math compared to PPS rates of 25 and 19, and Latino students are at 57% proficiency in ELA and 61 in math versus 33 and 25 at other PPS schools. The results are strong enough that PPS should not treat closing Glencoe as academically neutral, research reinforces the need for scrutiny. The University of Chicago Consortium found that outcomes after school closures depended heavily on receiving school quality, where students go and what education conditions they lose matter. If the district is not looking at academic data when they make their decisions, I fear you all have lost the plot. I respectfully ask the board to require three safeguards: to add an academic equity and educational continuity indicator for every school because academics matter to us. Prove that school closure is necessary by publishing a receiving school scenario alongside any closure scenarios. Compare subgroup outcomes, service continuity, receiving school capacity, travel distances, unique focal students affected, total students moved, and net savings.

Slow down and show us more data. Before eliminating successful schools, schools are at the heart of every community, and shutting them down should be the last possible resort. This is not a request to protect Glencoe by shifting harm to another school, nor to leave Glencoe unchanged. This is a request to preserve communities. These are children, not numbers. The amount of disruption to families and community members that even one school closure would create would rattle us. Closing anything close to 20 would devastate us. It would devastate Portland in a way I don't think we could recover from. Thank you. Thank you.
